title: Container and Resource Discovery
summary: Container and resource discovery is the enumeration of a container environment to learn what is running, which images exist, and how the platform is arranged. Attackers query the Docker or Kubernetes APIs, read platform logs, or use a web dashboard to list containers, pods, deployments, nodes, namespaces, and overall cluster status. Docker logs in particular can disclose configuration details, which services are reachable, and even which cloud provider hosts the workload. Kubernetes API responses include service accounts, references to secrets, and workload definitions that show where privileged workloads live and which nodes matter. The findings shape the next step, such as which container to enter, which node to target for an escape, or which service account to use for lateral movement. Detection uses API audit logs, where repeated list and get requests stand out, and runtime telemetry showing enumeration clients launched from inside a container rather than from an administrative host.

beginner.definition: Discovery means looking around to see what is present. In a container environment, this means listing containers, images, and cluster details. An attacker does this after getting a foothold. Those lists tell them where to go next.
beginner.whyItMatters: The platform already holds a map of everything it runs, and an attacker only has to ask for it. A single read request can reveal how the whole cluster is arranged. That knowledge turns a small foothold into a plan. If you never review API activity, the mapping happens silently.
howItWorks: The attacker lands inside a container, or steals a credential for the platform.
They ask the platform API for a list of containers and images.
They also list nodes, namespaces, deployments, and the accounts that run them.
Log files from the platform may reveal settings, neighbours, and the cloud provider.
From these lists they pick a target, such as a powerful container or a busy node.
The platform audit log records each request and the identity that made it.
beginner.example: Imagine starting a new job and being given a few minutes alone in the office. You read the noticeboard, glance at the seating plan, and note which doors need a manager badge. Nobody stops you, because walking around looks completely normal. Later you know exactly which room to visit and when it will be empty. The information came from ordinary things that were left on display.
takeaways: Platform APIs hand out a detailed map to anyone with read permission.
Discovery usually comes before lateral movement and escape attempts.
List and get requests in audit logs are the main detection point.

objectives: Explain what resources can be enumerated in a container environment.
Describe how Docker and Kubernetes APIs expose that information.
Explain why platform logs and dashboards are useful to an attacker.
Identify audit log patterns that suggest discovery activity.
Summarise how discovery findings shape later lateral movement.
